summary: A tight two-to-four-player area-majority game where players secretly place influence cubes to sway which of three factions (or all four with foreign invaders) will control regions, then race to remember what everyone actually committed since much of it is played face-down. It plays fast and mean, with a distinctive memory element that rewards tracking opponents' hidden bids as much as spatial strategy.
praised: Clever memory mechanic where you must recall face-down/hidden commitments rather than rely on open information
Tight, fast playtime (30-45 min) with high replayability from variable setup
Elegant, minimalist design that hides real depth
Strong player interaction and tension despite the small footprint
Second edition's improved components, art, and the new asymmetric advanced mode
criticised: Memory requirement can frustrate players who dislike memory-based mechanics or feel it punishes forgetfulness over strategy
Rules and interactions (especially multi-faction/backstab dynamics) take a play or two to click
Can feel swingy or kingmaker-ish in some player counts, especially with only 2-3 factions in play
Relatively abstract/dry theme layered thinly onto the mechanics

interaction.kind: blocking, hidden bidding, and area-majority maneuvering with a memory-tracking element

scoring.why: The winner is determined by which faction ends up dominant and whether that outcome favors your secretly held allegiances, not by accumulating points from multiple sources

_name: The King Is Dead: Second Edition
